title: Shaping integrity: why generative artificial intelligence does not have to undermine education
extended_summary:
This paper is an opinion/theoretical article that addresses a broad question: whether generative artificial intelligence (GAI) necessarily undermines academic integrity in education, or whether it can be integrated in ways that support learning and ethical practice. The authors frame the problem around widespread concern that tools such as ChatGPT may enable plagiarism, shortcut learning, and disrupt traditional assessment, while arguing that these risks should be understood alongside opportunities for more authentic assessment, digital literacy, and student motivation.

Rather than reporting an empirical intervention, the paper proposes a conceptual argument grounded in ethical and educational theory. It draws on deontological ethics, consequentialism, constructivist learning theory, and self-determination theory to argue for responsible AI integration. Across illustrative examples, the authors describe possible uses of AI for formative feedback, writing support, interactive simulations, collaborative project work, and assessment redesign. In particular, the paper mentions AI helping students revise drafts and receive immediate guidance, but these are hypothetical or literature-based examples rather than a tested ChatGPT feedback intervention on student-authored drafts.

No actual participant sample is studied. The discussion references educational contexts including high school classes, language arts, science, history, business, engineering, medical education, and higher education, but these are examples used to support the paper's argument rather than empirical settings with reported outcomes. Because of this, there is no reported subgroup, moderator, or comparative analysis by baseline writing proficiency, English learner status, struggling writers, disability status, grade level, gender, school achievement level, subject area, or writing genre. There is also no reported follow-up or delayed posttest evidence on unaided writing after feedback removal, independent revision skill, self-efficacy, confidence, metacognition, authorial voice, plagiarism rates, or overreliance in a studied sample.

The main conclusion is that GAI does not have to erode academic integrity if used transparently, ethically, and in alignment with sound pedagogy. The authors argue that AI can support intrinsic motivation, personalized learning, authentic assessment, and digital literacy, provided institutions establish clear ethical guidelines, invest in educator professional development, and iteratively evaluate implementation. The paper therefore contributes a normative framework and practical recommendations, not causal evidence about outcomes for secondary students using ChatGPT-generated feedback on drafts.
quality_tier_rationale: This is explicitly labeled an opinion article and does not report an original empirical study, sample, analytic design, or measurable outcomes. Although peer reviewed, it provides no direct methodology or evaluative evidence for the target secondary-school ChatGPT feedback use case.
impact_tier_rationale: Impact is unclear because the paper makes theoretical and ethical arguments rather than estimating effects. It discusses possible benefits and risks of generative AI in education, but provides no direct causal or quantitative evidence of impact.

interventions.use_case: Opinion paper discussing generative AI/ChatGPT as a classroom support tool that can provide immediate guidance, interactive responses, and personalized assistance across subjects, including draft support and formative feedback.
Conceptual discussion of AI-driven formative feedback on student drafts and other work products, including real-time guidance for revision, grammar, tone, and narrative structure.
Generative AI writing assistant for language arts/creative writing that analyzes student-authored text and provides feedback on grammar, tone, narrative structure, and possible revisions.
Referenced as an example of AI-enabled personalized learning through tutoring systems that adapt to student needs, though not directly evaluated.
Referenced as an example of AI-enabled personalization through adaptive content and pacing, but not empirically studied in this paper.
